To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We present MAESTRO, a large, high-quality, and high-resolution dataset for training neural networks to transcribe, compose, and synthesize music.

(i) we introduce a novel dataset of piano performances that enables the modeling of piano music at all timescales and that (ii) by using this dataset, we train a suite of novel models for transcribing, composing and synthesizing piano music at multiple timescales.

we introduce a new dataset of piano recordings with high-resolution alignment between audio and note labels, which we use to train a set of neural models that can transcribe piano music, compose new pieces, and generate expressive audio waveforms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. Can a neural network model learn a coherent and interpretable representation for music, one that captures the musical structure of the piece and the expressive qualities of its performance? If so, can this representation be used to generate novel music?
the development of neural networks for music modeling and generation, which is a challenging problem due to the need for modeling structure at many time scales (i.e., from milliseconds to minutes).
developing neural models of music that can learn and generate music in a variety of ways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we present a new dataset and models that allow for the generation of musical audio directly from a neural network, and the models can be trained on the dataset to create music.
we present a novel approach to modeling and generating music with neural networks, which is enabled by a new dataset of piano performances.
the paper presents a dataset of piano performances that are synchronized with MIDI note annotations and a set of models that can generate audio from MIDI note sequences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can now generate music with neural networks that is as good as a virtuoso pianist.
we have created an intermediate representation of music (notes) which allows for better modeling of music at all time scales (micro to macro), and we have created the dataset to enable this.

we have created a large dataset of piano performances that are aligned to MIDI and audio, and we have used this data to train a variety of models that can be used for music transcription, generation, and synthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now train neural networks to learn to generate music in a way that is interpretable and controllable, and which can be used to create novel music that is coherent and structured.
the intermediate representation of music as notes is critical for modeling music at multiple timescales.
by using an intermediate note representation, we can enable a new class of neural models capable of modeling and generating musical audio with coherent musical structure at multiple timescales.
